Συνήδομαι γὰρ τῷ νόμῳ τοῦ Θεοῦ κατὰ τὸν ἔσω ἄνθρωπον.
Clear allusion: law of sin at war; law of the mind.
Cyril's text reads εὐχαριστῶ τῷ Θεῷ (Byzantine), not χάρις τῷ Θεῷ; covers 7:24–25a.
Text includes the Byzantine addition μὴ κατὰ σάρκα περιπατοῦσιν ἀλλὰ κατὰ πνεῦμα; translated as given.

choices.why: κατακιβδηλεύει (lit. 'debases, adulterates'): rendered 'exposes it as counterfeit', the sense required by the contrast with the law's role as counsellor.
καταβιάζεται (middle, active sense, as in u06-open κατεβιάζετο… ἡ σάρξ): 'forces it', the object being the mind of the preceding clause.
ἐκτόπους ἡδονάς: 'disordered pleasures' (lit. 'out-of-place'); kept the same in u06-rem-early.
ὁμολογεῖ χάριν after εὐχαριστῶ: χάρις here is gratitude, so 'gives all thanks', not 'grace'.

choices.term: τοῦ καὶ σοφοῦν ἰσχύοντος καὶ … ἀποφαίνοντος
choices.english: who is able both to make us wise and to make us stronger than evil
choices.why: τοῦ καὶ σοφοῦν ἰσχύοντος καὶ … ἀποφαίνοντος is genitive masculine and agrees with Χριστοῦ, not with the dative feminine χάριτι, so it is Christ 'who is able both to make us wise and to make us stronger than evil' (matching κρείττους γὰρ ἡμᾶς ἀπέφηνεν ὁ Χριστός below).

pass_a_gloss: [lemma tail, Rom 7:21] to do (poiein) the good (to kalon), that to me the evil lies near (parakeitai). Behold (athrei) again how wisely and with art (eutechnos) he accepts (apodechetai) the law (nomos), not as able to blunt (apamblunein) the goad/sting (kentron) of sin (hamartia), nor able to kill off (kataneukroun) the in us sin, but as only putting into (enienta) the mind (nous) the knowledge (gnosis) of the beneficial (to sympheron). For if, he says, evil lies near me as indwelling (enoikoun) the flesh (sarx), yet the law debases/brands as counterfeit (katakibdeleuei) it, bestows help (epikouria) and is thought counsellor (symboulos), not however also redeemer (lytrotes). But there is need for those sick with (arrhostousi) sin not of discerning only that the better befits them to do, but also of being able (dynasthai) to accomplish (katorthoun) what would be good and seem right to the law; as indeed for those wishing to be esteemed in battles bare and sole knowledge (eidesis) of tactics does not suffice, but if strength (to eusthenes) also be present, such would then scarcely (molis) be brilliant and looked at. So if the law teaches the skill in good things, but in no way helps the overreached (pleonektoumenoi) by unsinewing (aponeuron) sin, good because also teacher (didaskalos), not however would it fairly be reckoned equal to the grace (charis) through Christ, which is able both to make wise (sophoun) and to show us stronger (alkimoterous) than evil. [Rom 7:22] For I co delight (synedomai) in the law of God according to the inner man. As I said already, the mind thirsts for the free (to eleutheron), and longs to be rid of the slandered/condemned (diabeblemena), and crowns with highest honours the law as introducer (eisegetes) of the finest; but the nature of the flesh constrains by force (katabiazetai) into out of place (ektopous) pleasures (hedonai), the law of sin warring and pressing on; law of sin he says is the inborn movement (emphyton kinema), and what one might think the passion (pathos) of flesh love (philosarkia), as indeed he called law of mind its inclination (rhope) and will (thelesis) toward the good. [Rom 7:24-25a] Wretched I man; who will rescue me from the body of this death? I give thanks to God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Meanwhile he complains (schetliazei) and cries against the flesh; and body of death he calls the from earth and pleasure loving (philedonon), because the law of sin is sick (nosein) in it; and he says he seeks the one able to free from such evils, and so that fittingly (euaphormos) he may introduce to us the redeemer, that is Christ, to whom he confesses all thanks (charis); for through him we have been redeemed (lelytrometha), not of the flesh but of the death of the flesh; not having died, but freed from the death in the members (mele), that is from the savage (agria) pleasure in the members. For Christ showed us stronger than pleasure and sin. [Rom 7:25b; 8:1] So then I myself with mind serve (douleuo) law of God, with flesh law of sin. No condemnation (katakrima) therefore now to those in Christ Jesus, not walking according to flesh but according to spirit (pneuma). A long discourse (logos) has been worked out by him, testing (basanizonti) finely each of the things in us and the ways (tropoi) of the overreaching (pleonexia), which is customary to endure for the [continues: mind of man].
pass_b_english: “…to do what is good, evil lies close at hand for me” (Romans 7:21). Notice again how wisely and skillfully he approves of the law: not as able to blunt the sting of sin, nor as capable of putting to death the sin within us, but only as instilling into the mind the knowledge of what is beneficial. For if, he says, evil lies close at hand for me as something that dwells in the flesh, the law nonetheless exposes it as counterfeit; it grants its help and is understood as a counselor, but not also as a redeemer.

Yet those who are sick with sin surely need not only to know clearly that they ought to do what is better, but also to be able to accomplish whatever is good and seems right to the law. So too, of course, for those who wish to win distinction in battle, bare knowledge of tactics alone is not enough; only if strength is added to it would such men then, and scarcely then, be brilliant and admired. If, then, the law teaches skill in what is good, but in no way helps those who are overpowered by cutting the sinews of sin, it is good because it is also a teacher; but it could not fairly be counted equal to the grace that comes through Christ, who is able both to make us wise and to make us stronger than evil.

“For I delight in the law of God in my inner self” (Romans 7:22). As I have already said, the mind thirsts for freedom, longs to be rid of what stands condemned, and crowns the law with the highest honors as the guide to what is noblest; but the nature of the flesh forces it toward disordered pleasures, while the law of sin wages war and presses hard upon it (Romans 7:23). By the law of sin he means the inborn impulse, and whatever one might suppose the passion of love for the flesh to be, just as he called the law of the mind its inclination and will toward the good.

“Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death? I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:24–25). For now he laments and cries out against the flesh; and he calls the earthly, pleasure-loving body a “body of death,” because in it the law of sin is a sickness. He says that he seeks the one who is able to free us from such evils, and he does so in order to bring in the Redeemer for us at a fitting moment, that is, Christ, to whom he also gives all thanks. For through him we have been redeemed, not from the flesh but from the death of the flesh; not by dying, but by being set free from the death in our members, that is, from the savage pleasure in our members. For Christ has made us stronger than pleasure and sin.

“So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin” (Romans 7:25). “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the spirit” (Romans 8:1). ποιεῖν τὸ καλὸν, ὅτι ἐμοὶ τὸ κακὸν παράκειται. Ἄθρει δὴ πάλιν ὡς σοφῶς καὶ εὐτέχνως
ἀποδέχεται τὸν 208 νόμον, οὐχ ὡς τῆς ἁμαρτίας τὸ κέντρον ἀπαμβλύνειν ἰσχύοντα,
οὔτε μὴν κατανεκροῦν οἷόν τε τὴν ἐν ἡμῖν ἁμαρτίαν, ἀλλ' ὡς ἐνιέντα μόνον τῷ νῷ τὴν
τοῦ συμφέροντος γνῶσιν. εἰ γὰρ ἐμοί φησι παράκειται τὸ κακὸν ὡς ἐνοικοῦν τῇ σαρκὶ,
κατακιβδηλεύει γεμὴν ὁ νόμος αὐτὸ, χαρίζεται τὴν ἐπικουρίαν καὶ νοεῖται σύμβουλος,
οὐ μὴν ἔτι καὶ λυτρωτής· δεῖ δὲ δὴ πάντως τοῖς ἀῤῥωστοῦσι τὴν ἁμαρτίαν, οὐ τοῦ
διειδέναι μόνον ὅτι τὰ ἀμείνω προσήκει δρᾶν αὐτοὺς, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῦ δύνασθαι
κατορθοῦν ἅπερ ἂν εὖ ἔχοι καὶ τῷ νόμῳ δοκῇ· καθάπερ ἀμέλει καὶ τοῖς ἐθέλουσιν
εὐδοκιμεῖν ἐν μάχαις οὐκ ἀπόχρη πρὸς τοῦτο γυμνὴ καὶ μόνη τῶν τακτικῶν ἡ εἴδησις,
ἀλλ' εἰ προσυπάρχοι τούτῳ καὶ τὸ εὐσθενὲς, εἶεν ἂν οἱ τοιοίδε τότε δὴ μόλις λαμπροὶ
καὶ ἀπόβλεπτοι. οὐκοῦν εἰ διδάσκει μὲν ὁ νόμος τὸ ἐν ἀγαθοῖς εὐτεχνὲς, κατ' οὐδένα δὲ
τρόπον τοῖς πλεονεκτουμένοις ἐπικουρεῖ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ἀπονευρῶν, καλὸς μὲν ὅτι καὶ
διδάσκαλος, οὐ μὴν ἔτι καὶ ἐν ἴσῳ χάριτι τῇ διὰ Χριστοῦ καταλογισθείη ἂν εἰκότως, τοῦ
καὶ σοφοῦν ἰσχύοντος καὶ ἀλκιμωτέρους ἡμᾶς ἀποφαίνοντος τοῦ κακοῦ. Συνήδομαι γὰρ
τῷ νόμῳ τοῦ Θεοῦ κατὰ τὸν ἔσω ἄνθρωπον. Ὡς ἔφην ἤδη, διψᾷ μὲν ὁ νοῦς τὸ
ἐλεύθερον, καὶ τῶν διαβεβλημένων ἀπαλλακτιᾷ, καὶ ταῖς ἀνωτάτω τιμαῖς στεφανοῖ τὸν
νόμον ὡς τῶν καλλίστων εἰσηγητήν· καταβιάζεται δὲ εἰς ἐκτόπους ἡδονὰς ἡ τῆς σαρκὸς
φύσις, πολεμοῦντός τε καὶ ἐγκειμένου τοῦ νόμου τῆς ἁμαρτίας· νόμον δὲ ἁμαρτίας εἶναί
φησι τὸ ἔμφυτον κίνημα, καὶ ὅπερ ἂν ὑπάρχειν οἴοιτό τις τῆς φιλοσαρκίας τὸ πάθος,
καθάπερ ἀμέλει καὶ νόμον ἔφη νοὸς τὴν εἴς γε τὸ ἀγαθὸν αὐτοῦ ῥοπήν τε καὶ θέλησιν.
209 Ταλαίπωρος ἐγὼ ἄνθρωπος· τίς με ῥύσεται ἐκ τοῦ σώματος τοῦ θανάτου τούτου;
εὐχαριστῶ τῷ Θεῷ διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν. Τέως δὲ σχετλιάζει καὶ
κατακράζει τῆς σαρκός· καὶ σῶμα θανάτου, τὸ ἀπὸ γῆς καὶ φιλήδονον καλεῖ διὰ τὸ
νοσεῖν ἐν αὐτῷ τῆς ἁμαρτίας τὸν νόμον· ζητεῖν δὲ λέγει τὸν δυνάμενον τῶν τοιούτων
ἀπαλλάξαι κακῶν, καὶ ἵν' εὐαφόρμως ἡμῖν εἰσαγάγῃ τὸν λυτρωτὴν, τουτέστι, Χριστὸν,
ᾧ καὶ τὴν πᾶσαν ὁμολογεῖ χάριν· δι' αὐτοῦ γὰρ λελυτρώμεθα, οὐ τῆς σαρκὸς, ἀλλὰ τοῦ
θανάτου τῆς σαρκός· οὐκ ἀποθάνοντες, ἀλλὰ τοῦ ἐν τοῖς μέλεσι θανάτου, τουτέστι τῆς
ἐν τοῖς μέλεσιν ἀγρίας ἡδονῆς, ἐλευθερωθέντες. κρείττους γὰρ ἡμᾶς ἀπέφηνεν ὁ
Χριστὸς ἡδονῆς καὶ ἁμαρτίας. Ἄρα οὖν αὐτὸς ἐγὼ τῷ μὲν νοῒ δουλεύω νόμῳ Θεοῦ, τῇ δὲ
σαρκὶ νόμῳ ἁμαρτίας. οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα τοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, μὴ κατὰ σάρκα
περιπατοῦσιν ἀλλὰ κατὰ πνεῦμα. Μακρὸς μὲν αὐτῷ ἐκπεποίηται λόγος, βασανίζοντι
λεπτῶς ἕκαστα τῶν ἐν ἡμῖν καὶ τῆς πλεονεξίας τοὺς τρόπους, οὓς ὑπομένειν ἔθος τὴν

review_notes: Agency/doctrine: τοῦ καὶ σοφοῦν ἰσχύοντος καὶ … ἀποφαίνοντος is genitive masculine and agrees with Χριστοῦ, not the dative feminine χάριτι, so Christ (not grace) is the one 'who is able both to make us wise and to make us stronger than evil'. Stiff calque 'acknowledges all his gratitude' (ὁμολογεῖ χάριν) made plain: 'gives all thanks'. British spellings (skilfully, counsellor, honours) brought to the book's American convention. Romans 7:21–25 and 8:1 (Byzantine text with εὐχαριστῶ and the 8:1 addition) verified; lowercase 'spirit' in 8:1 kept, since Cyril reads it as the mind's spiritual will (translator note).
Copy-text: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos via Khazarzar (Fragmenta in sancti Pauli epistulam ad Romanos.pdf).

Page numbers 208, 209 and the footer '15' are edition apparatus and are omitted.
